title: My Husband Insisted We Move to a Small Town in Maine. Then the Postmaster Handed Me 26 Years of Letters Addressed to Me (PART 2)

blocks.text: I drove home with the box on the passenger seat. Mark was in the garden. When he saw the letters, he sat down on the porch step and covered his face.

In 1999, I was a nineteen-year-old college student in Boston. Mark was my boyfriend. I got pregnant. We were scared but happy, and we planned to tell our parents at Christmas. In my eighth month, I filled out the hospital pre-registration forms and listed Mark as the person authorized to act for me and the baby. Two weeks later, I was hit by a car crossing a street in the snow.

I was in a coma for six weeks. Our daughter was delivered by emergency C-section while I was unconscious, at 4:17 in the morning. When I woke up, I had no memory of the previous fourteen months: not the pregnancy, not much of Mark.

The doctors told my parents the injuries meant I could never carry another child. Everyone agreed, in a terrible, well-meaning panic, that telling me I'd had a baby I couldn't remember would break me.

Mark was twenty-one, broke, and alone with a newborn. His older sister, Ellen, and her husband in Maine had been trying for a baby for years. They took her in, and eventually adopted her. Mark stayed in my life, slowly reintroduced himself, and married me five years later. He told me we couldn't have children. That part was true. He just never told me we already had one.
The letters were from Ellen. Every year on our daughter's birthday, she wrote to me, hoping that someday I'd know.
She sent them to the town post office "to be held for Catherine Ellis" because she didn't know how else to reach me without breaking her promise to Mark.
Ellen died last year. Before she died, she told our daughter, Grace, everything. Grace wrote to Mark and asked to meet her mother. That's why we moved to Maine.
"I was going to tell you," Mark said. "I've been going to tell you every day for twenty-six years."
I didn't speak to him for two days. Then I read every letter, all twenty-six, in order. I watched our daughter grow up through Ellen's eyes: first steps, braces, a softball trophy, a nursing degree.
I met Grace the following Sunday at a diner on the harbor. She's twenty-six, with my hair and Mark's terrible jokes. She brought the yellow blanket.
She said Ellen had always told her, "Your mother loved you before she ever saw you. She just got lost on the way home."
Mark and I are in counseling. Some days I'm furious. Some days I understand. Grace comes to dinner every Thursday. Last week she called me "Mom" by accident, and then didn't take it back.
